Let [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] be discrete random variables with supports [MATH: S_X] and [MATH: S_Y,] respectively. We say that [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] are independent if, for all [MATH: x\in S_X] and [MATH: y\in S_Y,] we have

Content:
[MATH: P(X=x, Y=y)=P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y).]

Content:
Moreover, if [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] have the joint probability mass function [MATH: f(x,y),] and [MATH: f_X(x)] and [MATH: f_Y(y)] are the marginal mass functions of [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y,] respectively, then

Content:
[MATH: f(x, y) = f_X(x)\cdot f_Y (y)]

Content:
for all [MATH: x\in S_X] and [MATH: y\in S_Y.]

Content:
If the random variables are not independent, they are dependent.

sections.normalized_html:
Two discrete random variables [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] with a joint probability mass function [MATH: f(x,y)] are independent if and only if

[MATH: f(x, y) = f_X(x) \cdot f_Y (y)]

for all possible values [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] where [MATH: f_X(x)] and [MATH: f_Y (y)] are the marginal probability mass functions for [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y,] respectively.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statement I is true. From the table, we obtain that [MATH: P({X = 0}, {Y = 0}) = f(0,0) = 0.24.] On the other hand, [MATH: P(X=0) \cdot P(Y=0) = f_X(0) \cdot f_Y(0) = 0.3 \cdot 0.8 = 0.24. \quad {\color{green}\checkmark}]

  • Statement II is true. Checking all other possible products, we obtain the following: [MATH: f(1, 0)|= 0.56 = 0.7 ⋅ 0.8 = f_{X}(1) ⋅ f_{Y}(0)|✓; f(0, 1)|= 0.06 = 0.3 ⋅ 0.2 = f_{X}(0) ⋅ f_{Y}(1)|✓; f(1, 1)|= 0.14 = 0.7 ⋅ 0.2 = f_{X}(1) ⋅ f_{Y}(1)|✓] So, [MATH: P({X = x}, {Y = y}) = P(X=x) \cdot P(Y=y)] for all possible [MATH: x] and [MATH: y.]

  • Statement III is true. Since statement II is true, our random variables [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] must be independent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

for all [MATH: x\in S_X] and [MATH: y\in S_Y.]
